newsitem.title: USA: NAACP members say police can't control hate groups.
newsitem.headline: NAACP members say police can't control hate groups.

text.p: It is unlikely that police are willing or able to control U.S. hate groups -- perhaps because many police officers are members of such groups themselves, several NAACP national conference participants said Wednesday.
"That's the problem. We have too many Ku Klux Klan members in the police," said Wendell Paris, a member of the NAACP's Mississippi chapter.
Deb Richardson, spokeswoman for the Fraternal Order of Police's national office in Washington, declined to comment on officers possibly being involved in hate groups.
"We're not going to dignify that with any kind of response," she said. "We don't believe it deserves one ... we have 277,000 members, including minorities. Our membership is very varied."
Constance Russaw of the NAACP's Michigan chapter said she agreed that some officers could be members of hate groups.

"I think there's bad in every organisation," she added. "In our community, the NAACP offered diversity training to the police department. The (white) officers said no; the only officer who showed up was black."
Arthur Wiley of the NAACP Virginia chapter said at the very least there likely is support among some police officers for hate groups and their racist messages.

"I think some police officers probably support most of these hate groups," he said. "But then again, I know of a black policeman who was arrested for selling drugs. What I'm saying is there are good and bad whites and there are good and bad blacks."
The NAACP debated several topics at this week's conference that affect minorities, including education, employment, police brutality and racism in schools and the military.
But several members focused on hate groups and said they believed those groups will possibly grow as African Americans continue to succeed in the public and private sectors.
Laurie Wood, director of Klanwatch and the Militia Task Force and a conference participant, said militia and hate group membership is rising.
"We estimate there are about 25,000 active white supremacists in the United States," she said.

Wood said 6,000 of that total are Klan members, 3,500 to 4,000 are skinheads, and the rest are members of other groups. Pennsylvania is home to 25 militia groups and said many states including California, Washington and Arizona, have 30 or more.
Meanwhile, the Klan announced its intention to make another appearance in Pittsburgh.

Edward Foster, Pennsylvania's grand dragon, said he and fellow Klan members will demonstrate Thursday. He said the demonstration will roughly coincide with President Bill Clinton's speech at the NAACP convention.
The Klan's last appearance in Pittsburgh was in April when about 40 Klansmen demonstrated in front of a hostile crowd.

Homer Floyd, executive director of the Pennsylvania Human Relations Commission, said contributing to the rise in hate-group membership was loss of jobs for underskilled white males, backlash against increased racial diversity of small communities, a large number of municipalities with limited law enforcement capabilities and weak laws regarding paramilitary training.

Cliff Savren, director of the Anti-Defamation League for Western Pennsylvania and Eastern Ohio, said while hate speech cannot be censored due to freedom of speech rights, there are things that have been done to curb hate groups.
Evelyn Hull Warner, education chair for the Pennsylvania NAACP, said her organisation is pushing schools to educate students about contributions by African Americans to the United States.
"The textbooks do not mention black contributions to this country," she said. "One of the things we can do is get involved in revising the books."
